definition: Gourmand means someone fond of eating and drinking.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word gourmand. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know gourmand should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A gourmand to his bones, my cousin plans road trips around diners the way other people plan them around monuments.
Foodie stops short of gourmand — a foodie photographs the tasting menu, while a gourmand orders it twice and means it.
Glutton goes further than gourmand — the gourmand eats for joy and stops at contentment's far edge; the glutton eats past pleasure into plain excess.

An epicure is a connoisseur of subtle pleasures, food above all — delight lies in discerning the quality most people miss. A gourmand's delight lies in the eating itself: appetite, abundance, and the joy of the table. The epicure hunts the perfect bite; the gourmand cheerfully finishes the platter.

A gourmet is a judge of food: refinement, technique, and quality are the whole point, and quantity is beside it. A gourmand is the eater rather than the judge — hearty love of eating and drinking itself, enthusiastically and in volume. The gourmet savors one perfect course; the gourmand happily orders seconds.

Gourmand is a whole-word French borrowing with a genuinely mysterious origin — no prefix, no root, no suffix to unlock. Its only 'relative,' gourmet, is a separate French word the centuries confused it with, so the pair must simply be memorized as neighbors: judgment on one side, appetite on the other.
Gourmand means someone fond of eating and drinking.

The food festival's organizers know their audience: gourmands who arrive at the opening bell with folding chairs, sample every stall twice, and compare notes on the brisket like scholars at a conference.

Gourmand is warmer than 'glutton' and humbler than 'gourmet' — a glutton eats past all pleasure, and a gourmet prizes refinement, while a gourmand simply loves eating and drinking, enthusiastically and in quantity.
Gourmand carries a wink — appetite as personality.
Gourmet praises taste; glutton condemns excess; gourmand sits between them, fond and a little indulgent.
Use it for the friend who plans the whole vacation around lunch.

Every chowder house on the wharf knows Captain Ilsa Brandt by her corner stool and her standing order: the big bowl, then another.
The food writer who came to profile her expected a critic's vocabulary and got a gourmand's grin instead.
'I couldn't tell you which broth is more refined,' Brandt said, tying on the bib.
'I can tell you I have never once left one unfinished.' She ate through the interview — crackers, both bowls, the pickle garnish nobody eats — and waved for coffee and pie.
The writer's notebook held one line by the end: appetite, joy, repeat.
